paragraphs.text: A loose [ripe pu’er](shou:definition) from Yunnan, made in 2009. At seventeen years it is well past the ten the trade counts as [aged ripe pu’er](shou:age-aged). The leaf goes on changing slowly with the air and moisture around it, which is why storage matters as much as the years.

Like all ripe pu’er, this leaf went through the [wet pile](shou:wet-piling). It was wetted, heaped and covered so the heat of its own microbes could work on it, turned about once a week to let air in, and dried after one to two months. The pile was developed to give in weeks what Hong Kong and Guangdong drinkers knew from raw pu’er aged for years. Yunnan’s state factories brought it into production in 1973, thirty-six years before this tea was made.

brewing.text: Ripe pu’er takes boiling water: fermented, tightly packed leaf needs full heat to open, and it does not scald the way green tea can. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and one quick rinse, which wakes the leaf and carries off dust and any pile smell. Then short steeps that lengthen as the leaf opens, so the cup stays clear rather than heavy; it gives eight or more good cups.

notice.text: A smooth, deep cup with woody, date-like or medicinal notes, which the trade calls aged aroma.
